name: Yusuf Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At fifty-eight I am one of the experienced hands on an electricity company line crew, though I still ask for a second check before we climb. My certificate and apprenticeship taught me to measure a damaged crossarm, fetch the right part and leave a clear record for the next shift. I like working beside a newer lineworker; long night callouts are what wear me out now. My partner and I have grown children and have been talking about finishing full-time work around sixty-five, if the retirement figures allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the same crews would build and repair power lines, with perhaps a quicker work order at the depot. I use AI now and then to tidy a parts note, but I check it against the damaged part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The typical lineworker wage and a few months saved make our household steady if shifts continue. I hope to finish full-time work around sixty-five, but I do not know the income figure yet and will not pretend I do. A tidy AI parts note cannot make the wrong bracket fit a damaged power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my repair shifts and compare each drafted parts note with the field measurements. This year my partner and I would request a retirement income estimate and set it beside our actual monthly bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the line work. The retirement sums still need doing, but modest AI does not move the date by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail in a parts note matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bracket size matters, because a neat note with the wrong size sends the truck back to the yard. I read the measurement from the field sheet before ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement estimate is too small for sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would look at continuing paid shifts, perhaps fewer nights if the company can offer them. I would not announce an exit until the sums cover our bills.

say: I would **welcome** shorter depot notes while keeping field measurements ahead of AI wording.
I would **keep** full-time repair shifts while checking retirement figures.
think: **Typical** pay and several months saved keep the household reasonably steady.
A **personal** target around sixty-five still depends on actual retirement income.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and compare parts notes with field measurements.
**Request** retirement income estimate and compare it with monthly bills.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary caution around retirement sums.
S0.quote: A tidy AI parts note cannot make the wrong bracket fit a damaged power line.
fieldNote: He **uses** AI occasionally for wording but gives field measurements priority.
His **planned** finish at sixty-five is conditional on real household income figures, not a promised statutory payment or fixed pension age.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and check parts notes against field measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that better booking may save a drive, but a dispatcher should not count an isolation check as wasted time. I would try a new schedule only after another crew has shown it works on real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office takes the first change, while my hands still repair lines. If the company trims callout hours, however, the pay we use to prepare for stopping at sixty-five could shrink before we are ready. A line repair near a school starts with barriers, not when a schedule says the wrench comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for a four-week comparison of the old and new callout schedules, including paid travel and isolation time. During the first year I would record any reduction in paid hours and take the figures to our household budget before changing the retirement target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost pay, because a convenient screen could quietly eat paid hours. I can see whether that happens before I make a large decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry in the schedule would you challenge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken line near a school needs barriers before the crew touches the pole. I would challenge any entry that starts the clock only when the actual repair begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the scheduling tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a colleague to demonstrate it on a real callout, then try entering a corrected isolation time on paid time. I would keep the paper work order until the new record proves reliable.

say: I would **test** scheduling on real callouts before trusting its time estimates.
A **full** work order must count barriers, travel and isolation.
think: **Field** repair stays useful, but lost callout pay could affect my retirement preparation.
I would **not** shift the sixty-five target without actual paid-hour figures.
do: **Compare** old and new schedules for four weeks.
**Learn** to enter corrected isolation times on paid scheduling tool.
**Record** any lost paid hours and review household budget before changing retirement target.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour cuts, with time to check records.
S1.quote: A line repair near a school starts with barriers, not when a schedule says the wrench comes out.
fieldNote: He is **open** to a proven tool but insists that paid preparation time remains visible.
His **occasional** AI use grows only after a colleague demonstrates the scheduling function.

steps.text: Learn corrected isolation entries on paid scheduling tool
Keep field work orders while comparing four weeks of schedules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes plans when I am sixty, and capable line robots around 2031 arrive when I am sixty-three. I would want a paid worker checking every isolation before a robot climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time at sixty-five if the numbers allow. Robots at sixty-three could cut two years of wages, and one to six months of savings would not bridge that gap if callouts really vanished. A line robot at sixty-three could take two working years from a plan aiming for sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request two written retirement estimates now, for finishing at sixty-three and sixty-five. In the first year after 2028 I would compare them with household bills, and if the sixty-three income is sufficient and callout hours actually fall, I would bring my full-time finish forward by two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the robot date lands inside my working plan. I have choices to check, but I cannot fill two years with a few months of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sixty-three estimate is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe line shifts and ask about paid ground inspection work if climbing became too much. I would not retire early just to get away from a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid isolation worker do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named crew member would check the physical isolation, mark the work sheet and stop the robot if the measured line disagrees with its plan. That needs to be a paid job, not an extra duty after shift.

say: **Thinking** AI may alter plans by 2028; robots could reach live lines around 2031.
A **paid** worker should check isolation before robots climb.
think: At **sixty-three** a robot could cut two years of intended wages before my conditional sixty-five finish.
**Several** months saved cannot bridge two years if callouts disappear.
do: **Request** written retirement estimates for sixty-three and sixty-five.
**Compare** both estimates with household bills after 2028.
**Bring** full-time finish forward only if early income suffices and callouts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible two-year wage gap, with figures to check.
S2.quote: A line robot at sixty-three could take two working years from a plan aiming for sixty-five.
fieldNote: His **early** retirement response is conditional on actual income and lost callouts.
The **age** dates come from his personal plan, not an assumed pension rule.

steps.text: Bring full-time finish to sixty-three if income suffices and callouts fall
Keep safe line shifts if early retirement income is too low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2031 changes dispatch when I am sixty-three, while capable line robots around 2034 arrive at sixty-six. If the household figures let me stop full-time at sixty-five, robots would reach the pole after I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year either side of sixty-five matters more to me than a shiny machine. If retirement income comes up short, I may still need paid work at sixty-six and would rather do measured ground checks than storm climbs. A robot arriving after my planned lineworker finish helps only if the retirement sums cover the kitchen bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would update the retirement estimate each year and ask the company this year what a paid ground inspector shift would involve. If the sixty-five figure covers bills, I would keep line shifts through 2031 and aim to finish around 2033, at sixty-five; if it does not, I would apply for a posted ground role at a wage that covers the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the money figure, but less worried about the robot timing. Five years gives us time to see whether our own plan adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ground check can you do without climbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could verify parts against the field sheet and inspect the completed repair record before the crew closes the job. I would need an actual paid assignment with clear responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company has no ground role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the few nearby electricity company vacancies and their written pay before leaving my crew. I would not move for a title that fails to cover our bills.

say: **Robots** around 2034 may arrive after my conditional full-time finish at sixty-five.
I would **still** want paid ground inspection options if income is short.
think: An **inadequate** retirement figure could keep me earning at sixty-six.
**Ground** checks would suit me better than more storm climbs then.
do: **Update** retirement estimates annually against household bills.
**Keep** line shifts through 2031 if safe and retirement remains affordable.
**Apply** for posted ground inspector work if retirement income falls short and pay covers gap.
feel: **Uneasy** about income details, less pressed by robot timing.
S3.quote: A robot arriving after my planned lineworker finish helps only if the retirement sums cover the kitchen bills.
fieldNote: He **sees** a possible timing advantage but refuses to assume retirement is funded.
His **fallback** ground role requires a posted paid assignment, not an imagined vacancy.

steps.text: Keep safe line shifts through 2031 while checking retirement figures
Apply for posted ground inspector work if retirement income falls short and pay covers gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 should give a line apprentice time to learn real fault work first. I would like to spend some of my remaining paid shifts showing younger workers how to read damaged hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight for thinking AI and seventy-one for robots, I might be out of full-time work if the sixty-five income plan holds. I cannot guarantee that today, but this timetable gives our household time to check rather than rush. A robot manual cannot replace an apprentice measuring the cracked crossarm beside a power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and ask the crew lead this year for one paid apprentice demonstration each month. If the retirement estimate still covers our bills at sixty-five, I would finish full-time then; if not, I would continue suitable paid work and review the figures again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machine date, with the normal caution about retirement money. It feels good to pass on a trade while I can still demonstrate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you demonstrate to the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show how a cracked crossarm changes the bracket choice and make the apprentice measure it before ordering. A robot manual will not teach that by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach after leaving full-time work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps if the company offers a paid session and I am fit enough, but I would decide from the actual hours and family budget. I would not promise free regular work.

say: A **decade** lets apprentices learn physical repairs before robots reach lines around 2039.
I would **teach** damaged hardware checks during paid shifts.
think: At **sixty-eight** I may already be out of full-time work if my sixty-five income plan holds.
I **still** need real retirement figures rather than an assumed entitlement.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and arrange monthly paid apprentice demonstrations.
**Finish** full-time at sixty-five if retirement income covers household bills.
**Continue** suitable paid shifts if the income estimate remains short.
feel: **Calm** about later robots, while checking retirement arithmetic.
S4.quote: A robot manual cannot replace an apprentice measuring the cracked crossarm beside a power line.
fieldNote: He **values** apprenticeship teaching while keeping it within paid current shifts.
**Leaving** at sixty-five follows his existing conditional plan, not a new early retirement decision.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and arrange paid apprentice demonstrations monthly
Finish full-time at planned sixty-five if retirement income covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable line robots around 2031 could take callouts two years before my hoped-for full-time finish. Written retirement estimates and a paid isolation role if I need more wages would help. My power line apprenticeship taught me repairs; it did not come with two years of replacement wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the experienced worker to stand beside a robot on its first live repair. A younger worker deserves a safe lesson, and I need that hour on the pay sheet if I am still working. A demonstration is only useful when the crew can stop it.

headlineQuote: My power line apprenticeship taught me repairs; it did not come with two years of replacement wages.
portrait: **Yusuf** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company lineworker whose vocational certificate and apprenticeship still guide his measurement of damaged hardware.
His **partner** and grown children are part of a household supported by typical wages and one to six months of savings.
He **uses** AI occasionally and accepts new scheduling only when paid preparation time remains visible on real callouts.
He **hopes** to finish full-time around sixty-five if retirement income permits; the fast robot date could bring that forward conditionally.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots around 2031, two years before his provisional full-time finish.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** retirement comparisons and paid isolation work if he needs more wages would help him choose.
